Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

T-4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

T-4. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

stories.headline: NRL: Spencer Leniu signs with Eels after early Roosters release
stories.summary: Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in their 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith from 2021-2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 per year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The westward move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Eels general manager of football Mark O'Neill shared his delight at signing one of the game's "premier enforcers".

"We're thrilled to have Spencer join the Parramatta Eels and become part of what we're building at this club," O'Neill said in a statement.

"He's one of the elite middle forwards in the game and has consistently performed on the biggest stages throughout his career.

The exit of Leniu adds to the exodus of stars from the Roosters premiership lineup.

Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Leniu had been a strong contributor during his time at the club.

"Spencer has brought a lot to our group over the last three years, both through the way he plays and the energy and personality he brings every day," Robinson said in a statement on Thursday.

"He brings an intensity and competitiveness to everything he does, and he challenges the people around him to be better.

"To see him finish his time here as a premiership winner is something he should be really proud of, and something we'll always share together."

With his departure announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

""I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," said Leniu.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."

stories.headline: Everton's Martin Sherif fined for breaching FA betting rules
stories.summary: Everton youngster Martin Sherif has been fined for breaching Football Association betting rules.
stories.body:
Everton youngster Martin Sherif has been fined for breaching Football Association betting rules.

The 20-year-old, who is yet to make a first-team debut for the Toffees, admitted having caused, permitted or enabled 61 bets to be placed on football matches between November 2024 and February this year.

Sherif has avoided a ban but must pay a £5,000 ($6,600) fine.

In his defence, the forward said he had not personally placed any of the bets, which totalled almost £2,000 ($2,600), but admitted they came from accounts in his name.

An independent regulatory commission hearing took into account Sherif's prompt admission of guilt after he was charged in August, his cooperation with the procedure and his "genuine remorse."

Sherif, a Netherlands youth international who joined Everton aged 13, spent last season on loan at Rotherham and Port Vale.

He scored two League One goals for each club across 24 total appearances.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton aspires for more wet-weather racing: FIA and young drivers 'more cautious'
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton feels the caution of Formula 1 bosses and its younger drivers has taken away some of the sport's "seat of your pants" wet-weather driving.
stories.body:
Lewis Hamilton feels the caution of Formula 1 bosses and its younger drivers has taken away some of the sport's "seat of your pants" wet-weather driving.

The seven-time world champion was speaking in response to last weekend's shambolic scenes in Malaysia, which saw drivers effectively unable to power their vehicles in the wet conditions.

The Bahrain Grand Prix held at the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia was overshadowed as F1 bosses had to abandon the start when a number of drivers, including Max Verstappen and Hamilton, were struck by gremlins -- directly linked to the controversial 50-50 split between combustion and battery power -- on the formation lap.

The grid eventually limped back to the pit lane and the race got under way after a 53-minute delay. It later emerged that new software had to be downloaded to the cars.

As a result of the painstaking delay, the track was significantly drier than it was at the scheduled start time -- with cars deployed on a mixture of intermediate and slick tyres.

Full-wet tyres are seldom used in modern F1 and Hamilton was asked whether -- aside from the unprecedented software glitch -- a more conservative pattern has developed when it comes to racing in the rain.

"Wet-weather races aren't the same as we used to have, for sure," Hamilton said in Singapore ahead of this weekend's race.

"I've had great races, in 2008 in the rain, and ultimately back then we had more testing and we did have better tyres for the rain. I love wet racing more than anything else.

"I do think the guys running the show are far more cautious but then again the young drivers coming in are more and more cautious.

- F1 cars to get software update after Malaysia 'bug' to prevent repeat at future races

- Singapore Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions

- Valtteri Bottas cycles impressive 400km from Malaysia to Singapore Grand Prix: 'Snakes were pretty chill'

"Us old-school drivers are like 'let's get racing,' and more of the youngsters are like 'let's not race.' So they're [the FIA] getting two different bits of information, and they are super cautious as well.

"That's where I'm like 'let's get going.' That's where we really get to test ourselves. Is it more risky? Absolutely."

Hamilton has made a reputation as an outstanding wet-weather driver, highlighted by his brilliant 2008 win at Silverstone, and again showed his prowess to fight back to third having dropped to 18th after mistakenly starting on slick tyres.

"When I was out on the slick tyre, it was the trickiest conditions," Hamilton added.

"It was wet, I was on slicks, but I love that challenge. And that's what racing is, where you have to drive by the seat of the pants, and that's really where you can make the difference."

stories.headline: Every team's odds to win the 2026 World Series: Dodgers still favorites

Three of Major League Baseball's final four are set and leading the pack are the Los Angeles Dodgers, who have been the championship favorites since the preseason and have reached their shortest odds yet at +125. They'll face off against the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series, with Los Angeles a -160 favorite to win the series despite Milwaukee's home-field advantage. The Brewers show +310 odds to win it all this season.

Just ahead of them on the World Series odds board are the Tampa Bay Rays (+300), who dispatched the New York Yankees in three games. The Rays figure to be favorites in the American League Championship Series against either the Chicago White Sox (11-1) or Cleveland Guardians (20-1).

stories.summary: From the six 7 p.m. matchups all the way through Maple Leafs-Golden Knights at 10, here's what to watch.
stories.body:
It's Thursday, which means the NHL has a massive slate of games for fans to consume. This week there are 10 contests around the league, including six beginning at 7 p.m. ET.

From those six through to Toronto Maple Leafs-Vegas Golden Knights (with a 10 p.m. opening puck drop), here's a look at the key stats and storylines in each contest, along with betting info on broadcast details:

Philadelphia Flyers at Ottawa Senators

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | OTT -142, O/U: 5.5

Both of these teams made the playoffs last season -- and one of them looks like it will be right back in the mix again. Led by Tim Stutzle, the Senators look like the real deal and almost appear as though the clean break from Brady Tkachuk this summer was a wise move from management. The Flyers, on the other hand, have yet to earn a win this season, and their -12 goal differential is second worst in the league -- ahead of only the Flames, who are assuredly in rebuilding mode. Does the tide turn on Thursday? Full preview

Utah Mammoth at Boston Bruins

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | UTA -118, O/U: 5.5

The Mammoth burst onto the scene last year by earning the first playoff berth in franchise history and taking the eventual conference champion Golden Knights to six games in the first round. After some impressive performances in the first week of 2026-27, they've done nothing but gather support for their claim as a true contender. The next stop is in Boston, where the Bruins have had an uneven start: wins over the Rangers and Jets were followed by bad losses to the Wild and Senators. Which version of the B's shows up? Full preview

Dallas Stars at Buffalo Sabres

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BUF -115, O/U: 5.5

The appearance of the Stars on the schedule brings about bad memories about 1999 for many Sabres fans, although several key members of the current roster weren't born when Brett Hull's controversial goal won the title for Dallas. As currently constructed, both of these teams should find their way back to the postseason this spring -- and perhaps another matchup in the Stanley Cup Final. Full preview

Nashville Predators at Montreal Canadiens

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MTL -185, O/U: 6.5

Each team brings a 1-1-1 record to this showdown, although fans of one of the teams are probably a lot less happy about that mark than the other's. In addition to the identical records, both teams have been driven by their stars so far. Steven Stamkos is the Preds' leading scorer, with three goals and one assist, while Nick Suzuki leads the way for the Habs with two goals and four assists. Full preview

Minnesota Wild at Tampa Bay Lightning

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TB -148, O/U: 5.5

In the possible future world where these two clubs meet in the 2027 Stanley Cup Final, fans will have to look back to the early season for evidence of how they performed against one another. After this tilt, the pair will square off in Minnesota on Nov. 7, and then that's that. How likely is that Cup Final matchup? Stathletes projects it as having a 1.79% chance, which is 12th highest (Avalanche-Lightning currently leads the projections, at 7.17%). Full preview

Vancouver Canucks at Carolina Hurricanes

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CAR -325, O/U: 6.5

From one of the more likely Cup Final matchups to one of the least likely; the defending champs welcome the team that finished dead last in 2025-26. However, the Canucks haven't been the easy out that they were last season, with two wins in four games (and a one-goal loss to the Golden Knights). Carolina's Sebastian Aho was kept off the scoresheet in Game 1, but has four goals and three assists combined in the team's next three games. Does he stay hot in this one? Full preview

Chicago Blackhawks at New York Islanders

7:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NYI -185, O/U: 5.5

Had Connor Bedard not injured himself this offseason, this would have been a fun showdown between two of the game's most exciting young players. Instead, it'll just be Isles D-man Matthew Schaefer in the spotlight, as he continues to build on his impressive rookie campaign. And, as consolation, the Blackhawks do have a current rookie leading them in scoring, 2025's No. 3 pick Anton Frondell, with a goal and three assists through four games. Full preview

San Jose Sharks at St. Louis Blues

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+/Disney+/Hulu) | STL -130, O/U: 5.5

Last season, both the Sharks and Blues missed the final Western wild-card spot by four points. Ahead of opening puck drop, the Sharks are the current possessors of that wild card in the Western standings, with the Blues two points back. The good news for St. Louis fans: The team has 81 games remaining to make up that gap. Thus far, the Blues have been led in scoring by two offseason additions -- Connor McMichael and Mason McTavish -- while San Jose has been paced by Macklin Celebrini, who missed the recent loss to the Stars and is listed as "day-to-day" on the injury report. Full preview

Colorado Avalanche at Calgary Flames

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -218, O/U: 6.5

Another game with lopsided expectations (as evidenced by that DraftKings line). Perhaps the simplest way to demonstrate: The Avs are averaging seven goals per game; at their current pace, the Flames won't score seven goals total until Game No. 7 this season. The Avs are allowing 2.5 goals per game; the Flames allow that many every 28 minutes. In other words, fantasy managers will want to be sure all of their Avs are in the active lineup -- even beyond the no-brainers like Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar and Martin Necas. Full preview

Toronto Maple Leafs at Vegas Golden Knights

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | VGK -162, O/U: 6.5

Maple Leafs-Golden Knights games last season took on added emphasis due to Mitch Marner's departure from Toronto to Vegas in summer 2025. That's less of a storyline this season; instead, this game will be another good litmus test for the Leafs as they push for a playoff return after last season's disappointment. This is not one of the more likely Cup Final matchups -- Stathletes projects it as a 0.02% chance -- but that number would assuredly rise if the Leafs keeping winning. Vegas' Jack Eichel leads all NHL scorers heading into Thursday, with 10 points through four games. Full preview

New hockey fans -- and maybe some veteran ones too -- might wonder why Florida Panthers fans throw plastic rats on the ice after home games.

ESPN's Kristen Shilton explored the origin of the tradition in this story, best summarized by this paragraph:

stories.headline: What does your NBA team need? The biggest hole on all 30 rosters
stories.summary: Every NBA team is missing something, even the leading title contenders.
stories.body:
In the NBA's second apron era, deep rosters don't stay deep forever, team identities can flip at a moment's notice, and money can prompt painful divorces.

This summer alone, the 2026 champion New York Knicks lost beloved backup center Mitchell Robinson, the 2025 champion Oklahoma City Thunder shed three rotation players in cost-cutting trades, and the 2024 champion Boston Celtics traded away Finals MVP Jaylen Brown. Meanwhile, the Minnesota Timberwolves sacrificed frontcourt depth to assemble a tantalizing backcourt duo, and LeBron James said goodbye to the Los Angeles Lakers after eight seasons.

Let's take stock of all 30 teams now that the offseason dust has settled and the preseason is in full swing. With so many salary cap rules preventing teams from aggregating talent, everybody is missing something, even the leading title contenders. But what, exactly, is each team's biggest hole?

Jump to a team:

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE

DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND

LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN

NO | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX

POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS

Atlanta Hawks
Roster hole: Superstar centerpiece

The Hawks have methodically constructed a balanced rotation with healthy doses of ballhandling, outside shooting and on-ball defense. After adding championship experience by nabbing Luguentz Dort and Aaron Wiggins from the Oklahoma City Thunder in offseason trades, Atlanta's biggest question is whether Jalen Johnson can elevate from All-Star to superstar.

The do-everything forward saw his impressive regular-season numbers dip dramatically in a first-round series loss to the Knicks, but he's still only 24 years old. Can he develop into an offensive fulcrum capable of leading a deep playoff run?

The Hawks can be patient in their assessment as they boast enough salary cap flexibility and draft assets to explore a big-name addition down the road.

Johnson is entering the second year of a team-friendly extension worth $150 million over five seasons, and none of Atlanta's other core pieces are on the books for more than $25 million this season.

Boston Celtics
Roster hole: Free throw generator

While the Celtics' decision to trade Brown for Paul George made sense as a long-term financial play, it created two immediate problems on the court. First, the 36-year-old George played less than half as many minutes as the 29-year-old Brown last season. Second, George attempted only 111 free throws in 2025-26 -- a far cry from Brown's 536, which easily represented a career high.

George's perimeter shooting and experience playing off high-usage stars should make him a good fit next to Jayson Tatum in coach Joe Mazzulla's 3-point heavy system, but Boston will need to find a way to replace Brown's ability to work inside the arc and draw contact. The Celtics ranked last in free throw attempts last season even though Brown ranked fifth in the NBA.

Tatum is the most obvious candidate to pick up the slack, but he's still trying to get back to full form after a 2025 Achilles injury. And don't ask center Mitchell Robinson for help; Boston's biggest offseason addition shot 40.8% from the stripe last season.

Brooklyn Nets
Roster hole: Starting center

Goodbye and good luck to Nic Claxton, who saw a bit of everything during his seven seasons in Brooklyn. The high-efficiency, low-usage center represented the right archetype during the Kevin Durant, Kyrie Irving and James Harden era, but he devolved into a forgotten man during the Nets' recent rebuild.

Brooklyn sent Claxton to the Chicago Bulls in a multiteam trade that returned three-time All-Star Julius Randle. By pairing Michael Porter Jr. with Randle, the Nets took a meaningful step to boost the 2025-26 season's worst offense.

But Brooklyn still lacks proven options at center to support its tandem of scoring forwards. Day'Ron Sharpe and Moritz Wagner are career backups, and the Nets appear poised to have a below-average defense for the seventh straight season.

Charlotte Hornets

Roster hole: Pass-first organizer

After stunning the NBA by jumping from 29th in offense in 2024-25 to fifth last season, the Hornets pivoted sharply by trading LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves in July. Ball led Charlotte in assists in each of the past six seasons, and his creative playmaking was a signature of the team's offensive identity.

Charlotte will take a by-committee approach to replace him. Kon Knueppel, Coby White and Dennis Schroder are all hybrid guards who can score and distribute, while forward Brandon Miller has untapped potential as a playmaker for his teammates. The Hornets still have enough offensive weapons to make a more egalitarian approach work, in part because Ball didn't quite measure up to the league's best offensive engines in terms of efficiency and impact.

But Hornets coach Charles Lee, a former Celtics assistant, is now faced with a dilemma that has long haunted Boston. While talented wings can help a team get by without a traditional point guard, it can be difficult to execute in late-game situations and in the playoff grind without a table-setter. For now, Charlotte is in position to absorb some growing pains given the youth of its top-end talent.

Chicago Bulls

Roster hole: Perimeter shooters

The Bulls will need some time to refine their roster after slamming the reset button with front office and coaching changes this offseason. New coach Tiago Splitter will emphasize a fast-paced approach with Josh Giddey running point and forwards Matas Buzelis and Caleb Wilson capable of finishing plays in transition.

But Chicago's half-court offense will almost certainly struggle due to its limited arsenal of outside shooters. Aside from Norman Powell, a career 39.6% 3-point shooter who arrived from Miami, the Bulls' projected starters range from "total non-shooter" (Claxton) to "a breakthrough is still possible" (Buzelis). Wilson wasn't a threat from beyond the arc as a University of North Carolina freshman, though he excited fans with his impressive marksmanship during his Las Vegas Summer League debut.

White, Ayo Dosunmu, Collin Sexton, Kevin Huerter and Anfernee Simons are all gone after logging minutes for Chicago last season, and Powell can't be expected to fill such a gaping void on the perimeter by himself. The Bulls ranked 18th in 3-point percentage and sixth in attempts last season. Both rankings will likely drop in 2026-27.

Cleveland Cavaliers
Roster hole: Playoff closer

The Cavaliers' 2025-26 season slipped away when they blew a 22-point fourth-quarter lead in Game 1 of the Eastern Conference finals against the Knicks, squandering a 31-point effort by star guard Donovan Mitchell. Unfortunately, that collapse furthered a recent trend of playoff heartbreak for the Cavaliers, who were upset by Tyrese Haliburton's Indiana Pacers in 2025, swiftly eliminated by the eventual champion Celtics in 2024, and bounced by the Knicks in the 2023 first round.

Though Mitchell reached a new milestone by leading a team to the conference finals for the first time in his nine-year career, Cleveland was left to ponder whether its expensive and veteran-dominated roster will ever be able to get over the hump. Rather than shake up the core group or change coaches, the Cavaliers kept the band together and added forward Peyton Watson to address what had been its biggest starting lineup hole.

Once the Cavaliers elected to run it back, the pressure returned to Mitchell, Harden and Evan Mobley to deliver a Finals run. The 37-year-old Harden showed his age by averaging 4.7 turnovers in the 2026 postseason, and Mobley struggled to take over in close games due to his limited shot-creating ability and range. Mitchell remains Cleveland's best option to play hero, but his recent playoff track record suggests he's at risk of being outdueled by rival stars.

Dallas Mavericks

Roster hole: Backcourt playmaking

The Mavericks' new regime took its first steps to reorient the organization around 2025 No. 1 pick Cooper Flagg by hiring coach Dusty May, drafting physical forward Morez Johnson Jr. and trading for 2024 No. 1 pick Zaccharie Risacher. With Kyrie Irving back after missing last season while recovering from knee surgery, Flagg should be a strong All-Star candidate and the Mavericks should be fighting for a play-in tournament spot.

While May has compared Irving to Pablo Picasso, the first-time NBA coach must understand that his dazzling All-Star guard is best deployed in a score-first role. The Mavericks' grinding offense ranked 27th without Irving last season, but heaping full-time point guard responsibilities on the 34-year-old guard is a recipe for disappointment and additional health concerns. Flagg, 19, should also be spared from the burden of running the offense on a possession-to-possession basis as he continues to mature.

Guard Sergio de Larrea flashed some impressive passing skills at Las Vegas Summer League, but he's a 20-year-old rookie who played in Spain last season. Don't be surprised if the Mavericks make a midseason move to add a veteran point guard capable of initiating possessions and making life easier for Flagg and Irving.

Denver Nuggets

Roster hole: Peyton Watson

Let's not overthink this. The capped-out Nuggets could really use an energetic 24-year-old forward who can defend multiple positions, contribute offensively in a complementary role and shoot 41% on 3-pointers. Well, they had exactly that player in Watson before sending him to the Cavaliers in an August sign-and-trade.

Denver's decision to prioritize cost cutting made it clear that ownership wasn't fully committed to competing for a championship. Because the Nuggets received only future draft picks and no replacement wings for Watson, three-time MVP Nikola Jokic must now try to make it work with young guards Christian Braun, Spencer Jones and Julian Strawther.

The Nuggets did add DeMar DeRozan on a veteran's minimum contract in free agency, but the 37-year-old forward doesn't offer the defensive energy or floor spacing needed to properly support the core trio of Jokic, Jamal Murray and Aaron Gordon. Denver is left to hope Braun enjoys a big bounce back after a poor 2025-26 campaign.

Detroit Pistons
Roster hole: Secondary playmaker

The Pistons filled a $200 million hole in their frontcourt by inking All-Star center Jalen Duren to an extension last week, ending a standoff that lasted all summer. Duren's return doesn't guarantee Detroit will be among the East's top contenders again, but it should prevent the upcoming season from being derailed by drama and hard feelings.

With Cade Cunningham, Duren and Ausar Thompson all in place with long-term contracts, Detroit boasts an elite lead playmaker and an imposing defensive identity. The Pistons also took steps to improve their offensive spacing by adding John Collins and Isaiah Joe this offseason.

But Detroit still lacks a dependable secondary playmaker to support Cunningham. After Tobias Harris departed in free agency, Cunningham was left as the Pistons' only returning player to average at least 12 points per game in the 2026 playoffs. Thompson, 23, should get more opportunities to create this season, but he must improve his shaky ballhandling and atrocious outside shooting.

Golden State Warriors

Roster hole: Jimmy Butler III

The Warriors were smart to hold training camp in Hawai'i; there's no better place to forget life's problems.

Most of Golden State's shortcomings can be traced back to Butler's torn ACL, which cut short his 2025-26 campaign in January and is expected to sideline him for the first few months of the upcoming season.

With Butler on the shelf and owed $56.8 million this season, Golden State suffered through a quiet offseason highlighted by an extension for franchise guard Stephen Curry and the arrival of lottery pick Yaxel Lendeborg. The Warriors, who won 37 games last season, struck out in their pursuit of LeBron James and were unable to land any other difference-makers.

Lendeborg, 24, looks poised to assume a starting role, but the Warriors' playoff hopes will rely on Butler making an immediate impact once he returns. While he declared on media day that he's posting "staggering" results on his rehabilitation testing, the 37-year-old forward's offensive game is predicated on physicality and drawing fouls. Modest expectations are in order.

Houston Rockets

Roster hole: Floor-spacers

Fred VanVleet's return from a seasonlong knee injury should help improve the Rockets' flow and stability on offense, but it might not solve their spacing concerns. Houston ranked 28th in 3-point attempts during the 2025-26 regular season and dead last in 3-point percentage during the playoffs.

The Rockets wisely hired renowned shooting coach Chip Engelland away from the Thunder in July, and he will have his hands full. VanVleet is a respectable outside shooter, but Houston won't reach its ceiling unless it gets dramatic 3-point shooting improvement from Amen Thompson (21.6% last season) and Alperen Sengun (30.5%).

Houston's relative inactivity this summer suggests its decision-makers are banking on meaningful internal development. The Rockets' biggest offseason addition was free agent guard Marcus Smart, a veteran stopper with a career 32.4% clip from 3. One young candidate who could help ease the crunch is Reed Sheppard, an undersized guard who has gradually earned more playing time from defensive-minded coach Ime Udoka.

Indiana Pacers

Roster hole: Backup center

The Pacers didn't sit around last season as they waited for Haliburton to recover from an Achilles injury. Instead, they filled the biggest hole in their lineup by replacing outgoing center Myles Turner with Ivica Zubac. The productive 7-footer, who arrived via a trade with the LA Clippers, should improve Indiana's rebounding and feast on Haliburton's brilliant setups.

Otherwise, Indiana stuck with a feisty rotation that stunned the basketball world during a 2025 Finals run. Pascal Siakam, Aaron Nesmith, Andrew Nembhard, T.J. McConnell, Obi Toppin and Jarace Walker are all still in place and ready to flank their electric point guard.

The Pacers' questionable interior depth, which was exposed at times by the Thunder during the 2025 Finals, remains a concern. Indiana's frontcourt was regularly bullied last season, and coach Rick Carlisle doesn't have many great options behind Zubac. If Haliburton hits the ground running and has the Pacers back in the playoff picture, perhaps the front office can line up some fortifications at the trade deadline.

LA Clippers

"Roster" hole: Steve Ballmer

No team has a bigger hole to fill than the Clippers, who must operate without Ballmer after the NBA handed him a yearlong suspension in September following an investigation into salary cap circumvention. Until Ballmer's suspension runs its course, LA-based attorney John S. Gibson, a Clippers season ticketholder, will serve as the team's interim governor.

Ballmer, the NBA's richest owner, has been active and engaged throughout his tenure, and his absence will loom large over a franchise in transition. LA has entered a rebuilding cycle after trading Kawhi Leonard (to Toronto), Harden (to Cleveland) and Zubac (to Indiana) since February, but the Clippers' ability to replenish took a big hit when they were forced to forfeit five first-round picks as part of the league's punishment.

The new-look Clippers, who will open the season without injured forwards Brandon Ingram and Max Strus, project as a lottery team due to their lack of size, physicality and cohesion. Beyond this season, it's hard to imagine the franchise will be able to chart a clear course until Ballmer is back in the saddle.

Los Angeles Lakers
Roster hole: Proven starting forwards

Look, there's going to be a little less positional certainty whenever LeBron departs. Rather than target a single replacement for the four-time MVP, the Lakers invested their resources into re-signing guard Austin Reaves, acquiring starting center Walker Kessler and compiling a grab-bag collection of unproven forwards with varying skill sets.

In his season tipoff news conference, Lakers coach JJ Redick said that both starting forward spots would be up for grabs. Redick's long list of options includes Quentin Grimes, Matisse Thybulle, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Ziaire Williams, Jake LaRavia, Jarred Vanderbilt and Adou Thiero.

Regardless of who wins the job, the Lakers will ask both forwards to function as high-activity defenders and auxiliary options in an offense led by Luka Doncic and Reaves. As the season unfolds, Redick will be in position to compensate for his lack of standout forwards by extending his rotation with a "quantity over quality" approach.

Memphis Grizzlies

Roster hole: High-usage scorers

How quickly did Memphis undertake a complete roster makeover? When the 2024-25 Grizzlies won 48 games and reached the playoffs, they had four players average at least nine shots per game. All four -- Ja Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr., Desmond Bane and Santi Aldama -- will be playing elsewhere this season.

This season will be spent defining roles and figuring out which of the next generation of Grizzlies should be taking all those available shots. Grizzlies coach Tuomas Iisalo has prioritized pace, ball movement and scoring balance, so don't be surprised if his team's pecking order needs time to materialize.

Cameron Boozer, the No. 3 pick in June's draft, will likely be given a green light as a scorer and playmaker, and Cedric Coward, a 2025 lottery pick, should get the opportunity to smooth out the rough edges in his offensive game. From there, Ty Jerome and Scotty Pippen Jr. are a functional guard duo, while veteran forward Jerami Grant arrives from Portland with several years of experience as a volume scorer on bad teams.

Miami Heat

Roster hole: Backcourt creators

Naturally, Miami's roster tilts toward the frontcourt thanks to the new pairing of Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. The All-Star big men give the Heat an imposing foundation on both ends, and they will create nightly matchup problems for opponents.

To ensure Antetokounmpo has sufficient room to operate offensively, the Heat prioritized perimeter shooting by signing free agents Klay Thompson and Tim Hardaway Jr. and by drafting Ryan Conwell in the second round. But Miami's offense is still at risk of bogging down because its rotation is light on backcourt creators.

Davion Mitchell, a 2021 lottery pick who cut his teeth as a defensive stopper, is the roster's X factor and should see an expanded role as an initiator. Past that, coach Erik Spoelstra will likely need to lean on Adebayo's capable passing to compensate for a guard rotation that's short on pop after trading Tyler Herro in the Antetokounmpo deal.

Milwaukee Bucks

Roster hole: Giannis Antetokounmpo

Antetokounmpo's departure for Miami after 13 seasons in Milwaukee left a Grand Canyon-sized hole in the Bucks' rotation and in the city's heart. After years as a perennial playoff team, Milwaukee is plunging into a rebuild with a quality new coach in Taylor Jenkins and an incredibly random roster.

Really, the Bucks have two rosters mashed into one: There are the holdover role players (Myles Turner, Gary Trent Jr., Kevin Porter Jr.) who were collected to help Antetokounmpo win in recent years, and then new role players (Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel'el Ware, Kasparas Jakucionis) from Miami who made up the return package for the two-time MVP. Outside of Herro, a borderline All-Star guard, there's not much in the way of top-end talent. And Bucks fans will shudder if the inconsistent Kyle Kuzma steps into Antetokounmpo's starting power forward spot.

Given that there's no way to replace or quickly move on from a franchise icon, Milwaukee's attention should shift to carefully tracking the development of 2026 lottery picks Brayden Burries and Nate Ament. Ryan Rollins, a scoring guard who emerged as a pleasant surprise last season, should also help provide some cheery moments amidst the gloom.

Minnesota Timberwolves

Roster hole: Frontcourt depth

Many of the best playoff moments from this highly successful era of Timberwolves basketball came courtesy of a deep frontcourt rotation that could wear down Nuggets star Nikola Jokic and overwhelm less physical opponents. First, it was Rudy Gobert, Karl-Anthony Towns and Naz Reid. Then, it was Gobert, Reid and Julius Randle.

Now it's just the 34-year-old Gobert and some fresh faces. Minnesota shifted course this summer by sacrificing some of its frontcourt depth to acquire guard LaMelo Ball. The Timberwolves had needed another backcourt creator next to franchise guard Anthony Edwards for years, so the pivot solved one problem even as it potentially opened a new one.

Without Reid and Randle, the Timberwolves will turn to 2025 first-round pick Joan Beringer as a backup to Gobert. The 19-year-old French center was a Las Vegas Summer League standout, but he still must prove he can handle all the responsibilities that come with rotation minutes in the playoffs. Minnesota will also need Gobert's excellent availability to continue in his 14th season: The four-time Defensive Player of the Year has appeared in at least 70 games each of the past four seasons.

New Orleans Pelicans

Roster hole: Franchise player

Zion Williamson offered a candid self-assessment on media day as he prepared to enter his eighth season: "I'm not where I want to be. I'm not where I need to be."

It's safe to say that just about everyone shares his disappointment.

The Pelicans weathered several injury-plagued seasons and have given Williamson every opportunity to lead a winner. While last season represented a step forward from an availability standpoint, Williamson's lack of 3-point range and defensive limitations undercut his powerful scoring ability and athletic tools. Even if the 2019 No. 1 pick played all 82 games, it's unclear whether he could achieve the superstar potential that many analysts envisioned when he was a Duke standout.

Sticking with Williamson has left New Orleans juggling lineup fit questions and competing interests. The Pelicans need to play a center alongside Williamson to support him defensively, but that cramps offensive spacing. They need to put the ball in his hands, but that can come at the expense of their scoring-minded guards. The Pelicans' problems start at the top.

New York Knicks

Roster hole: Backup center

The Knicks will enjoy exceptional continuity as they launch their title defense, returning nine of the top 10 players from their 2025 Finals rotation. What's more, New York's returning players logged 93.7% of the minutes during the team's five-game Finals win over the Spurs. It's hard to beat that.

Of course, the lone departure of significance was backup center Mitchell Robinson. With Knicks owner James Dolan signaling his desire to avoid the second apron, the beloved rebounding specialist signed a three-year, $47 million contract with the Celtics after eight years in New York. The Knicks then filled his spot by inking Andre Drummond to a one-year, $3.9 million deal.

Will the difference between Robinson and Drummond cost New York its chance at back-to-back championships? Probably not. But New York will have a tougher time weathering any absences from Towns.

Oklahoma City Thunder
Roster hole: Wemby-stopper

The Thunder traded away three of their seven players who logged at least 1,400 minutes last season and somehow remain the NBA's most complete team, even though they only got draft picks in return. That feels impossible.

Cason Wallace, Ajay Mitchell and Jared McCain are poised for larger roles after the departures of Luguentz Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins, and Oklahoma City added 2026 lottery pick Aday Mara to a deep and balanced frontcourt rotation. Of course, the Thunder are also counting on standouts Jalen Williams and Isaiah Hartenstein to enjoy better health than they did last season.

Even with all that talent around two-time MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, the Thunder don't have a great singular answer for defending Spurs star Victor Wembanyama. Chet Holmgren should be motivated to bounce back after an underwhelming showing in the West finals, but Oklahoma City has had more success getting physical with "The Alien" with a rotating crew that includes Hartenstein, Alex Caruso and Jaylin Williams. While the 7-foot-3 Mara presents another supersized option, Wembanyama clearly remains the biggest obstacle in Oklahoma City's title path.

Orlando Magic

Roster hole: Traditional point guard

Here's a telling nugget: 57 different players have averaged at least six assists per game since 2018-19, but none of them did so while playing for the Magic. In related news, Orlando hasn't ranked higher than 12th in offensive efficiency during that period.

Jalen Suggs looked like he would be the answer to the Magic's distribution problems when he was a top-five pick in 2021, but he's evolved into a defense-and-energy archetype as opposed to a two-way traditional point guard. That has forced forwards Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner to pick up some of the playmaking duties with mixed results.

Given that Orlando changed coaches this summer, the onus is on Banchero and Wagner to prove they can lift Orlando's offense to greater heights. If the so-so results continue, the Magic should consider reconfiguring their core with a lead guard who knows how to get everyone involved. It's been a while.

Philadelphia 76ers

Roster hole: Joel Embiid injury insurance

In their narrow first-round series win over Boston, the 76ers were plus-6 with Embiid, minus-20 with Andre Drummond and minus-27 with Dominick Barlow. Simply put, Philadelphia was just good enough to prevail when its franchise center was on the court and largely struggled to get by when his backups were called into duty.

Drummond departed for the Knicks this summer and newcomer Ariel Hukporti tore his Achilles in the preseason, leaving only Barlow and Adem Bona to provide depth behind the oft-injured Embiid. While the 76ers loaded up by adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown this summer, they're still at risk of being exploited inside when Embiid inevitably misses time.

James could potentially step in to play center in small ball lineups, but 76ers coach Nick Nurse will want to limit the wear and tear on the 41-year-old star during the regular season. Assuming the 76ers live up to expectations as one of the East's top contenders, they should spend trade season scouring the center market.

Phoenix Suns
Roster hole: Center

The Suns have tried to get by with budget-friendly centers as they rework their roster following Kevin Durant's 2025 departure. But that strategy took a hit in September when starter Mark Williams, the team's leader in rebounds and blocks last season, underwent surgery to repair a torn labrum.

With Williams expected to miss several months, coach Jordan Ott must turn to backups Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach, who have combined for just 31 starts in their brief NBA careers. Ighodaro, 24, is a fluid and versatile option who fits Ott's high-pressure style, while Maluach, 20, earned rave reviews at Las Vegas Summer League in July.

Unfortunately, the 6-foot-11 Ighodaro lacks the traditional size needed to handle the league's most physical centers, and the 7-1 Maluach must prove he has the stamina to make a meaningful impact after logging just 411 minutes as a rookie. The Suns' hopes of building on an unexpected 2026 playoff appearance are in jeopardy: They played at a 46-win pace with Williams in the lineup and a 41-win pace when he was sidelined last season.

Portland Trail Blazers

Roster hole: Sure hands

The Blazers led the NBA with 17.3 turnovers per game last season, a full 1.5 more than No. 2 Brooklyn. Remarkably, the gap between Portland and Brooklyn was equal to the gap between Brooklyn and the Sacramento Kings, who ranked 18th in the league with 14.3 turnovers per game. Everyone from All-Star wing Deni Avdija to rookie center Yang Hansen contributed to the gross display of giveaways.

This could be a tricky problem to fix, given that Portland will deploy a new offensive system under first-time coach Micah Nori and add veteran guards Damian Lillard and Ja Morant to a crowded backcourt. Lillard is getting back up to speed after missing last season with an Achilles injury, and Morant led the Grizzlies with 3.6 turnovers per game last season. With changing roles, lineups and systems, it's probably best to brace for turbulence early in the season.

There is a chance, however, that Lillard's experience running the show will eventually make life easier for Avdija, Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson. Avdija was overtaxed as a do-everything point forward last year, and Holiday and Henderson are best utilized in off-ball, defense-first roles.

Sacramento Kings
Roster hole: Plus defenders

The Kings should be applauded for plucking Ben Simmons out of Australia's competitive fishing scene and giving him a shot to revive his NBA career. While the former No. 1 overall pick has a lot to prove after sitting out last season, Sacramento's interest is an acknowledgment that it must explore every option to improve a dismal defense.

Sacramento ranked 28th in defensive efficiency last season and could drop even further this season with a roster that's light on point-of-attack stoppers and rim protectors. Domantas Sabonis' return from knee surgery should help improve Sacramento's rebounding, but the backcourt pairing of rookie Darius Acuff Jr. and Zach LaVine won't provide nearly enough resistance.

Russell Westbrook and DeMar DeRozan departed this summer, which could set the stage for a wider roster overhaul over the next 12 months. LaVine and De'Andre Hunter both hold large expiring contracts, and Sacramento should focus on surrounding the talented Acuff with as many young, versatile defenders as possible.

San Antonio Spurs

Roster hole: Closer

After a demoralizing Finals loss, the Spurs took a clear-eyed approach to fine-tuning their rotation. San Antonio addressed the weak link in its starting lineup by landing Tobias Harris to provide additional size and scoring pop at power forward.

In the draft, the Spurs selected big men Tarris Reed Jr. and Jayden Quaintance (sidelined indefinitely after knee surgery) to add size and toughness behind franchise center Victor Wembanyama and backup Luke Kornet. San Antonio carried too many aging 7-footers last season, and its new frontcourt pieces should enjoy a long runway to develop alongside the 22-year-old Wembanyama.

With all their kinks worked out on paper, the Spurs can turn their attention to the late-game collapses that doomed them in the Finals. Wembanyama must display better shot selection, decision-making and stamina when the game is on the line, but the Spurs must also decide which of their talented guards should be on the court during crunch time. De'Aaron Fox hardly looked like the 2023 Clutch Player of the Year during the Finals, and 2025 lottery pick Dylan Harper appeared to have the skill set and temperament to put a team on his back when needed.

Toronto Raptors
Roster hole: Center versatility

The Raptors moved off one regrettable contract when they traded Brandon Ingram for Kawhi Leonard, but Jakob Poeltl remains on the books for $104 million over the next four seasons. While the 7-foot center occupies the paint and works hard on the glass, he lacks the ability to stretch the court and doesn't function as a facilitator.

Those limitations led Toronto to reduce Poeltl's playoff minutes in favor of more versatile lineups. Scottie Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles excel at defending taller and longer opponents, and the Raptors' defense was at its best when coach Darko Rajakovic deployed the forwards together without Poeltl.

But those small ball configurations will take a toll on Barnes, who will continue to carry a heavy offensive load even after Leonard's arrival. Given that the Raptors lost a small ball center option when Sandro Mamukelashvili signed with the Lakers in free agency, they should prioritize adding another alternative to Poeltl before the playoffs.

Utah Jazz
Roster hole: Perimeter defense

The Jazz, who seem poised to turn the corner after a lengthy rebuilding period, have a deep collection of scoring talent. Lauri Markkanen, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Keyonte George have all averaged 20 points per game, and recent lottery picks Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey have the potential to hit that mark in the future.

But the most pressing question is whether Jackson can help lead a defensive turnaround after Utah ranked 29th last season. The Jazz traded projected starting center Walker Kessler to the Lakers this summer, betting that Jackson, the 2023 Defensive Player of the Year, and veteran center Jusuf Nurkic will be able to hold down the backline.

That plan should work if both big men can stay reasonably healthy, but Utah's perimeter defense is a different matter. George is a minus defender who is easily targeted by opposing guards; Peterson projects as a two-way standout, but he's still a 19-year-old rookie adjusting to the NBA game. While the Jazz nabbed stopper Josh Okogie in free agency, additional reinforcements will likely be necessary as this young core grows together.

Washington Wizards
Roster hole: Winning mentality

The Wizards enter the season with their most talented roster in years after selecting AJ Dybantsa with the No. 1 overall pick and trading for All-Stars Trae Young and Anthony Davis last season. While Washington didn't make any splashy moves after the draft, they brought back wise veteran Khris Middleton and filled out their frontcourt rotation with center Deandre Ayton.

Draftniks will marvel that the Wizards have accumulated three No. 1 overall picks (Davis, Ayton and Dybantsa), a No. 2 pick (Alex Sarr), a No. 5 pick (Young), a No. 6 pick (Tre Johnson), a No. 7 pick (Bilal Coulibaly) and a No. 14 pick (Bub Carrington). Remarkably, former lottery picks account for more than half of Washington's 15-man roster.

But Carrington hit on the central challenge of Washington's season when he told WUSA9 recently that the team's young players had been "held back" last season as the franchise maximized its chances to land Dybantsa. Flipping the switch from "tanking" to "trying hard" is more difficult than it sounds, especially for a franchise with so little recent success.

It's time for the entire Wizards organization to get serious about making progress in the standings.

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs 2026: After another early exit, what's next for Fever?
stories.summary: Despite a dominant offense and Caitlin Clark's return, the Fever suffered another early playoff exit. What's next for Indiana?
stories.body:
INDIANAPOLIS -- A week ago, ahead of a deciding Game 3 against the Las Vegas Aces, Indiana Fever forward Myisha Hines-Allen laid out the franchise's expectations plainly.

"There's always going to be room for growth, but with how [GM] Amber [Cox] put this team together, it's championship or bust," Hines-Allen said before the game. "We're all trying to win this championship this year."

After a semifinal appearance in 2025, a season in which star Caitlin Clark sat out most of the year injured, hopes were high for 2026.

And sure enough, the Fever had the No. 1 offense in WNBA history, averaging 96.0 points per game in the regular season. Kelsey Mitchell (24.7 points per game) and Clark (22.3) finished ranked No. 2 and No. 3 in points per game and were the highest-scoring teammates in league history.

But throughout, off-court drama surrounded the team. Then a swoon in the final days of the regular season dropped the Fever to the No. 6 seed, facing the defending champion Aces in a best-of-three first round.

After the Game 3 loss, a back-and-forth affair, the Fever were left reckoning with a season that ended earlier than any of them hoped.

Within 48 hours of the season-ending loss, another controversy had developed: After Cox issued a strong defense of the Fever fanbase in her end-of-season availability, Mitchell seemed to contradict it, referencing troubling fan behavior and the intense microscope that comes with playing alongside Clark. It was a fitting conclusion to a season of big dreams and bitter disappointments where the focus could never just be on basketball.

"Not every season's perfect," Aliyah Boston said Saturday after the season's end. "You're going to have your ups and downs, but we really stuck together through it all. Like no matter what. Obviously, when you look back at games that you wish that you didn't drop early, and maybe that would have been a difference. ... But here we are, right? There's nothing we can do right now."

ON THE COURT, at least one half of the Fever's plan went perfectly.
The offense was formidable, and Clark's return went better than anyone could have hoped. Mitchell set the league record for the most points scored (1,086) and the most 3-point field goals (135) while scoring 20-plus points in a WNBA-record 27 consecutive games. Boston was an All-Star for the fourth consecutive year with a career-high 16.1 points per game, grabbed 8.0 rebounds and extended her range beyond the 3-point line and shot 40.6%.

Clark was the first player in the history of the league to score 40-plus points with 10-plus assists in a single game; her five games of 30-plus points and 10-plus assists this season are more than any other player in league history combined. She became the league's first player to record 800-plus points and 300-plus assists in a single season.

Clark called 2026 one of the most fulfilling years of her career. She played more basketball than ever as she rehabbed. She played in Team USA camps, 40 regular-season games and was selected for the FIBA World Cup team that won gold in September. A worrisome back issue flared up early in the season but proved not to be a long-term issue. The defensive part of her game was highly criticized early in the season as teams specifically targeted her, but even that improved incrementally. A sneaky midrange game began to appear as the season went on to complement the drives to the basket and the step-back 3s.

Clark's first signature shoe with Nike, the Caitlin 1, released last week.

"I didn't play much last year, but I was able to come out here and put together the best season I've had," Clark said, "and perform at a really high level and basically get better in every area and still feel like I have so many areas to improve.

"I guess that's the most exciting part moving forward."

The old saying, though, goes that defense wins championships, and that was the problem all season for the Fever. They ranked No. 11 in points allowed per game (90.4) and No. 8 in defensive rating (108.3). The Aces scored 102 and 94 in Game 1 and 3 victories to eliminate Indiana.

And off the court, the Fever were constantly barraged with distractions or drama. For much of the season, it felt like those 40 minutes between the lines -- win or lose -- were the most peaceful, normal times of the summer for this group.

"Obviously, we weathered a lot," Clark said. "There's always so much outside noise and a microscope of how we perform every single day, and a lot of really good moments, a lot of tough moments, too."

SINCE CLARK WAS drafted No. 1 in 2024, the Fever have had an inordinate amount of attention on the organization from both WNBA fans and entities that rarely paid attention to the league in the past. Clark's name was recently, and randomly, brought up in the middle of a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.

It's been a boon for the Fever, who have become the most popular team in the league thanks in large part to her fame -- quickly acknowledged by all those around the team, including Cox.

"The other piece about Caitlin that I never want to take for granted is just what she has meant to our team, what she has meant to the league, and what she's meant to women's basketball," she said. "She remains the tipping point. You look at the ratings and you look at the full buildings, that started in 2024 when she came into the league, and that is because of Caitlin Clark."

But it can also lead to increased scrutiny on Clark and the rest of the team, as happened multiple times this season.

In June, the relationship between Stephanie White and Clark was questioned after the coach was seen in an animated discussion with the point guard during a 16-point loss to the Portland Fire. Both downplayed it as two competitive people in the heat of the moment. Clark and assistant coach Briann January also had fiery interactions on the sideline that begat questions regarding the franchise player and the coaching staff.

The focus on the Fever's play -- and White -- continued throughout the season. Then, in June, Sophie Cunningham kicked off another round of headlines for the Fever. Cunningham, a popular personality on social media and her podcast, has no problem being an agitator. T-shirts featuring her pointing at DeWanna Bonner after a heated game against the Phoenix Mercury in June became a hot commodity at Fever games at home and on the road.

But one moment affected not only the Fever, but the entire league. In an ESPN article published in July, Cunningham discussed, among other things, how to "protect women's sports" and said: "I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

It became a seasonlong topic with coaches and players being asked their opinions around the league. Protests both for and against began forming outside arenas when the Fever would play on the road. Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton was suspended from attending five home games after her exchange with a pair of fans who brought signs into Climate Pledge Arena supporting Cunningham with the Fever in town for a road game in late July.

All these issues and more -- 11 Republican lawmakers sent WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert a letter in July demanding the league take "accountability" for "multiple attacks" against Clark -- came to a head just after the All-Star break.

In a game on Aug. 8, Cunningham took a hit around the head and neck on a fast-break layup from DiJonai Carrington. The particularly hard contact started a dustup on the court; Carrington was issued a flagrant 2 and ejected from the game. Moments later, Carrington posted on her Threads account: "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever." Postgame, White acknowledged it was a hard foul, but said she didn't think Carrington intentionally went for the neck.

Fever fans accused White of not supporting her players. Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith tweeted, "Ok... The @IndianaFever need to let Stephanie White go. No solid coach would ever take the side of the opposing team's player who committed a flagrant foul on one of your own players. Terrible coaching! The Fever need to defend their players."

During the next home game, on Aug. 11 against the New York Liberty, boos rained down on Gainbridge Arena. The disdain was focused on White during pregame introductions. Before that game, White had used her pregame media session to respond to the noise; team president Kelly Krauskopf issued a statement with full support for White that same day.

"The hate, the fearmongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win," White said before the game, pounding her fist on a table multiple times.

"We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," she added. "Every day, these women put their ass on the line. Every day, when they go low, we go high. Love will win, grace will win, humility will win, and kindness will win. I stand by them. I will always stand by them.

"Everybody else can go to hell."

EVERY SEASON WITH Clark on the team will have championship expectations, a side effect of having a generational player on the roster. But every season with Clark, through no fault of her own, also brings a level of outside noise that organizations will have to navigate.

That was evident on Saturday, during Mitchell's end-of-season availability.

Compared with her interviews after the Game 3 loss, the weight seemed lifted from Mitchell's shoulders as she smiled and acknowledged that she would be "selfish" in her approach to unrestricted free agency.

Mitchell -- the Fever's No. 2 player in points and assists, No. 1 in 3-point field goals and No. 4 in steals in franchise history -- said it's hard to play in Indiana due to fan behavior and the intense microscope that comes with playing alongside Clark.

"Showing up every day to compete for fans that may or may not like you is hard," Mitchell said.

Earlier Saturday, in her own availability, Cox had effusively praised Clark and ended her session with a staunch defense of Fever fans that have received criticism for their behavior toward opposing players.

"The attacks on our fanbase have no basis in reality, and they need to stop," she said.

(Former Fever player Brianna Turner, now a member of the Aces, disputed Cox's sentiments on social media. "This is an unequivocally false statement," wrote Turner, who serves as treasurer of the Women's National Basketball Players Association. "Players inside and outside the organization have repeatedly issued complaints with the Fever fanbase. While it's not all Indy fans, it's certainly a trend. To say the attacks have 'no basis in reality' is disingenuous.")

Along with Mitchell, Cunningham, Tyasha Harris and Hines-Allen are all unrestricted free agents this winter -- meaning, like everything in the orbit of the Fever, the offseason could be dramatic.

Cox has said her priority is bringing back Mitchell and keeping the Fever's Big Three together.

Clark's play has made her eligible for the "EPIC" (Exceptional Performance on Initial Contract) provision of the new collective bargaining agreement that allows players to renegotiate the fourth year of their rookie deal and sign a three-year extension. Players that have been named all-WNBA first team or second team are eligible for a max deal or the supermax if named MVP.

"Caitlin has earned the opportunity to sign her EPIC extension, so we're really excited to talk to her and her team about that," Cox said. "She had an MVP-caliber season, and it was wonderful to see coming off of her injury."

As for Cunningham, Cox said the off-court conversations surrounding her will not impact the evaluation of the player. Through the first two months of the season, Cunningham was considered a Sixth Player of the Year candidate before she cooled over the last two months. Both Cox and White pointed to help on the wing as an offseason priority.

"Sophie's had two really productive years for us in terms of shooting the basketball," Cox said. "She is a really solid leader in the locker room, a great connector. She brings levity, but also brings a lot of experience. She's serious and is an important voice in our locker room when we need it. When we really need to lock in.

"She's an unrestricted free agent, so we look forward to having those conversations. Again, she had a really productive year, and we'll see just where things take us."

White, too, will be part of the conversations about the Fever's future. She just finished her second year at the helm, and 2025 was considered an overachievement, advancing to within one game of the Finals with an infirmary ward of a roster. The last five months have been considered a disappointment with a first-round exit and questions swirling around her job stability.

"There were some highlights, and there are things we never need to get better at," Cox said after the season. "We're all going to get in the room and get back to the drawing board and we're going to address some of those and make sure that we're ready to go when next season starts. And that includes Steph and the coaching staff."

"I feel support from the organization, no doubt about that," White said after the season. "At the end of the day, it's their decision about whether I return or not. I'd love the opportunity. I love this this franchise. I have always felt supported from this franchise, and I hope to continue to be the coach."

This all awaits Cox in what will undoubtedly be another busy offseason. A new practice facility is scheduled to open before 2027 training camp. Cox wants to add frontcourt depth to help Boston and Makayla Timpson, and a three-and-D wing is also on the wish list. Despite expectations, the Fever were light on playoff experience and there's optimism that it was gained the hard way. The hope is to continue to develop the young talent, build through the draft and supplement through free agency.

After a season with unfulfilled goals and more drama than anyone was thrilled about, there's an understandable wonder of how much could change.

"When you talk about the noise around this team, I think that's just a product of becoming mainstream," Cox said. "People care. I've been a part of this league for many, many years, and you could have a trade, you could have a bad loss and nobody cared. Nobody was writing about it. Nobody was tweeting about it, and that was bad. Apathy was bad.

"So, what comes with the quote-unquote noise? I would call it just a lot of people caring."
